title: Regina Caeli
hook: in Eastertide it replaces the Angelus: rejoice, he is risen

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ave Regina Caelorum: the night song of Lent, a root, a gate, and a goodbye before sleep. Your line was hail, queen of heaven. Whom did you greet properly? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-seven.

Noon, and somewhere a church bell rings. For a lot of the year, the prayer that goes with that bell is the Angelus, which tells the beginning of the story: an angel, a young woman, a yes, and the Word made flesh. But from Easter to Pentecost, Catholics who keep the noon bell set the Angelus aside and pray something else. The story has jumped to its ending, and the prayer jumps with it. It's short, and every line ends in the same word, like a door that keeps swinging open: alleluia. Today's word is the Easter prayer to Mary, Regina Caeli.
screen: `NOON, AND A BELL.` → `THE ANGELUS TELLS THE BEGINNING.` → `IN EASTER, THE ENDING.`

segments.voice: Hear it a line at a time, in plain English. Queen of heaven, rejoice, alleluia. For he whom you were worthy to bear, alleluia, has risen, as he said, alleluia. Pray for us to God, alleluia. Start with the first command: rejoice. In Latin, laetare. Go back to this week: the woman who stood at the cross, whose soul Simeon said a sword would pierce. In the Easter prayer, the first thing said to her is be glad. The one who knew the worst of Friday is told about Sunday. Next, the two Latin words in the middle that carry the weight: sicut dixit, as he said. They echo the angel at the empty tomb in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "He is not here, for he is risen, as he said." The prayer doesn't only announce that he rose. It says he kept his word. A promise, made before the cross, turns out to be true on the other side of it. Then the alleluias. Through Lent, the Latin Church sets the word alleluia aside; it isn't sung at Mass. At Easter it comes back, and this little prayer can't stop saying it. Last, the prayer still asks: pray for us to God. Even at the height of joy, it ends by turning to Mary for help, the way this whole week has. So the noon bell, in Easter, rings for a mother told to rejoice because her son kept his promise.
screen: `THE FIRST WORD TO HER: REJOICE.` · `SICUT DIXIT: AS HE SAID.` · `ALLELUIA COMES BACK.` · `STILL ASKING: PRAY FOR US.` · then, large: `HE IS NOT HERE, FOR HE IS RISEN, AS HE SAID.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray it at noon in Easter. Whatever the season is now, rehearse it. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one promise someone made to you and kept. Small is fine: a friend who showed up, a parent who came back, a call returned. Let yourself remember the moment you knew they'd kept it. Then let it widen: as he said. If you pray, you can say the Regina Caeli now, slowly, with an alleluia at the end of each line, and set a reminder to pray it at noon when Easter comes, or the Angelus until then. If you don't, simply hold that kept promise in mind, and let it be good news. The bell holds the time.

Regina Caeli. Queen of heaven: the Easter prayer, rejoice, he is risen. This week's road: many names, poetry for a mother, comfort of the afflicted, mother of the church, star of the sea, hail, queen of heaven, and now rejoice. Today's word.
Your line: queen of heaven, rejoice. Today, keep one promise exactly as you said it, and tell one piece of good news to someone who needs it. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: In the Easter season, from Easter to Pentecost, Catholics who pray the Angelus at morning, noon and evening say the Regina Caeli in its place, and it also closes Night Prayer through that season.

original.note: Latin: queen of heaven, rejoice, the prayer's opening words.

trapdoor: what you thought: another title calling Mary a queen.
what it means: the Easter prayer that takes the Angelus's place: rejoice, he is risen, as he said, alleluia.
what a scholar hears: laetare addressed to the mother of sorrows, sicut dixit echoing Matthew 28:6, and alleluia returning after Lent sets it aside.
